algorithm: A **sequence of unambiguous instructions** for obtaining a **required output** for **any legitimate input** in a **finite amount of time** (slide 7). Miss any one part and it is not a valid algorithm. See [What an algorithm is](#/comp3760-l1/what-is-an-algorithm).
basic operation: The statement that **gets executed most frequently** in an algorithm (slide 27). We count only its executions; the count is the running time C(n). Ties are settled by the tie-breakers. See [Choosing the basic operation](#/comp3760-l1/basic-operation).
tie-breakers|tie-breaker|tiebreakers: When two lines run equally often: 1 function calls (growing with N), 2 function calls (constant time), 3 key comparisons, 4 assignments, 5 expression evaluations; multiplication/division before addition/subtraction; deepest inside the loop. Guidelines, not strict rules (slide 41).
key comparison: A comparison between two pieces of **data** (A[j] > v, A[i] = A[j], A[i] ≠ K), as opposed to a loop-counter test. Data comparisons are considered more expensive than simple numerical comparisons or assignments, so they usually win the tie-break (slide 37).
running time|C(n): The number of times the basic operation executes for an input of size n, written C(n) (or f(n) when every statement is counted). Always a function of n. See [Counting statements](#/comp3760-l1/counting-statements).
input size|n: The parameter the running time is measured against: number of list items, the number n itself, a matrix dimension. Step 1 of the textbook's general strategy.
worst case: The most possible number of steps an algorithm needs, over all inputs of size n. **Unless otherwise specified, always analyze the worst case** (slide 54). See [Best, worst and average case](#/comp3760-l1/best-worst-average).
best case: The number of steps needed if you "get lucky" with a particular input (sequential search finding K at A[0]: 1 comparison).
average case: The number of steps needed "on average" over the inputs of size n.
order of growth: How C(n) grows as n → ∞, ignoring constants and lower-order terms; what we really care about when comparing algorithms (slide 58). See [Order of growth](#/comp3760-l1/order-of-growth).
efficiency class: The tight order of growth of an algorithm's running time: constant, logarithmic, linear, n-log-n, quadratic, cubic, exponential, factorial (slides 60 to 61).
Big-O|big-O|O(g(n)): f(n) ∈ O(g(n)) if there are a constant c and a positive integer n₀ with **f(n) ≤ c·g(n) for all n ≥ n₀**: f is bounded **above** by a constant multiple of g. "Execution will take at MOST that long." See [Big-O, Big-Ω, Big-Θ](#/comp3760-l1/big-o-omega-theta).
Big-Ω|big-Omega|Ω(g(n)): f(n) ∈ Ω(g(n)) if **f(n) ≥ c·g(n) for all n ≥ n₀**: bounded **below**. "At LEAST that long."
Big-Θ|big-Theta|Θ(g(n)): f(n) ∈ Θ(g(n)) if **c₂·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c₁·g(n) for all n ≥ n₀**: bounded above and below, the same rate of growth. "THAT long."
logarithmic|log n: Class of algorithms that cut the problem's size by a constant factor on each iteration (i ← i/2). Such an algorithm cannot take into account all its input.
linear: Class n: algorithms that scan a list of size n, such as sequential search.
n-log-n|n log n: Class n log n: many divide-and-conquer algorithms, including mergesort and quicksort in the average case.
quadratic: Class n²: two embedded loops; elementary sorting algorithms and operations on n-by-n matrices.
cubic: Class n³: three embedded loops; several nontrivial linear-algebra algorithms.
exponential: Class 2ⁿ: algorithms that generate all subsets of an n-element set.
factorial: Class n!: algorithms that generate all permutations of an n-element set. 100! ≈ 9.3·10¹⁵⁷.
pseudocode: The "Common Tongue" of computing: variables, assignments, expressions, conditionals, loops, subroutines, written so that everybody can understand it. Used in lectures, the textbook, quizzes, labs and exams.
insertion sort|Loops: The lecture's Example 3 (Loops): for each i, shift larger earlier elements right until A[i] fits. Basic operation A[j] > v; worst case (n − 1)n/2 comparisons, best case n − 1.
sequential search: Scan a list for K, comparing each element until found. C_best(n) = 1, C_worst(n) = n; the count depends on the order of the input.
element uniqueness|UniqueElements: Check whether all elements of an array are distinct by comparing every pair i < j. Worst case n(n − 1)/2 = n²/2 − n/2 comparisons ∈ O(n²); best case 1.
